meta.title: Search Autocomplete
meta.summary: Suggest popular completions on every keystroke from a precomputed in-memory trie, rebuilt from search logs every hour.

functional: Return the top 10 completions for a typed prefix
Trending queries show up within about an hour
nonFunctional: < 100 ms p99 per keystroke, including the network

slos.sli: Suggest requests that succeed divided by all suggest requests

slos.name: Trend freshness
slos.sli: Trending queries appearing in suggestions within the threshold, divided by all trending queries

alerts.why: Search feels broken without suggestions, even though search itself still works.

alerts.when: p99 latency above 100 ms for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Suggestions must keep up with typing, or they are worse than none.
The hourly rebuild or the rollout is failing, and suggestions grow stale.

alerts.when: CDN hit ratio below 80% for 30 minutes
alerts.why: More requests reach the origin than the sizing assumed.

alerts.when: Trie build failed, or took over twice its normal time
alerts.why: Fix before the next rebuild, or the trie goes stale.

flows.title: Keystroke (cache hit)
flows.summary: Most prefixes are short and popular, so the CDN answers without reaching the origin.

steps.label: resolve search.example.com
steps.detail: Cached by the browser and by resolvers, so the lookup happens once per session and autocomplete keystrokes never wait on DNS.

steps.label: debounce 100 ms
steps.detail: Wait until typing pauses briefly. Fast typists send far fewer requests.

steps.label: HIT (max-age 300)
steps.detail: Prefix popularity follows a power law, so a few thousand short prefixes cover most traffic.

flows.title: Keystroke (cache miss)
flows.summary: A longer, rarer prefix reaches the origin, where one trie walk returns the precomputed answer.

steps.label: walk trie, read top-10
steps.detail: Each trie node stores its own top-10 list, so the lookup costs O(length of prefix). No subtree search, no database.

steps.label: log query
steps.detail: Only submitted searches are logged for popularity, not every keystroke.

steps.label: top 10
steps.detail: Now cached at this edge for the next five minutes.

flows.title: Hourly trie rebuild
flows.summary: Popularity is computed offline; serving nodes swap to a new snapshot without downtime.

steps.label: upsert decayed scores
steps.detail: score = old_score × decay + new_count, so trending queries rise fast and stale ones fade.

steps.label: build trie, top-k per node
steps.detail: Also filters offensive and policy-blocked phrases before they can be suggested.

steps.label: load trie-v1234 (rolling)
steps.detail: Instances load the new version one at a time and swap atomically in memory. Rolling back is loading the previous snapshot.

notes.text: If the trie no longer fits in one machine's memory, shard by prefix range (a-f, g-m, …) and route by first characters.
Caching responses for 5 minutes removes most origin load at the cost of a few minutes of staleness, which suggestions tolerate.
Offline rebuilds keep the serving path read-only and simple. Real-time trending needs a second, small, frequently updated trie merged at query time.
Serving nodes are stateless after loading a snapshot; a failed node is replaced and loads the latest version.
Personalization (your own recent searches) is usually a separate small per-user list merged in on the client or at the service.

questions.q: Suggestions must appear within about 100 ms of each keystroke. Where does that time budget go?
questions.a: Serve from memory: the suggest service holds the trie for the top prefixes, so a lookup is microseconds. Cache popular prefix responses at the CDN and in the browser, and debounce keystrokes on the client. The rebuilt trie is loaded from a snapshot, never queried from a database on the hot path.

questions.q: A breaking news term should start appearing in suggestions. How fresh can they be?
questions.a: The batch pipeline rebuilds the trie hourly, which is fine for most terms. For trending terms add a small fast path: a streaming counter over recent minutes whose top terms are merged into the results at query time. Freshness is a trade-off against cost and stability.

questions.q: How do you decide which completions to show for a prefix?
questions.a: Rank by query frequency with time decay so recent popularity counts more, and store the top K completions at every trie node so a lookup does not have to search the subtree. Personal history can be blended on the client or in a separate step. Filter offensive or unsafe terms before they enter the trie.

questions.q: The trie no longer fits in one server's memory. What do you do?
questions.a: Shard it by prefix range, for example by the first one or two characters, with a routing table that balances popular ranges. Each shard is replicated for availability. Trimming rare queries from the trie usually shrinks it a lot before sharding is needed.

questions.q: How do you roll out a newly built trie safely?
questions.a: Write the new snapshot alongside the old one, validate it (size, sample lookups), then have servers load it in the background and switch atomically. Keep the previous snapshot so you can roll back instantly if suggestions look wrong.

questions.q: Every keystroke could be logged. How do you keep the logging volume sane?
questions.a: Log completed searches, not every keystroke, and sample if needed; the ranking only needs relative frequencies. Aggregate counts in batches rather than writing one row per query. Drop personal data from what feeds the global suggestions.
